Colorado’s 4th District candidates clash as economic fallout hits local ranchers.
Lauren Boebert and Eileen Laubacher debate tariffs, the Iran war, and record inflation.
Evidence: Trade protectionism, Rural energy inflation, Partisan self-preservation #COpolitics #Debate 🌐

Boebert claims sweeping tariffs serve as an indispensable negotiating tool to secure American dominance, while standing unconditionally behind presidential war powers in Iran to deter nuclear threats without regime change.
Stated Judgement: (+0.84, +0.72) — Greater Good

Tariffs and war have driven diesel to record highs, hitting Eastern Plains farmers while strikes during peace talks killed 150 girls. Both candidates opportunistically moved districts to chase political survival.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.92, -0.95) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Destruction. Empty populist rhetoric and executive loyalty abdicate constitutional duty, leaving rural agricultural communities to absorb crushing energy costs and war shocks.
Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 18.50, z: 2)

- Boebert: FAIL (-0.92, -0.90) — Abdicates war oversight.
- Laubacher: COND (+0.15, -0.40) — Opportunist party swap.
- Tariffs/War: FAIL (-0.95, -0.92) — Crushes farm fuel costs.
- Denver Post: PASS (+0.70, +0.20) — Factual debate recap.

In Colorado’s 4th District debate, Rep. Lauren Boebert defended Trump’s Iran strikes and tariffs, while retired Rear Adm. Eileen Laubacher attacked rising farm costs and accidental civilian deaths amid record diesel inflation.

The Bright Side:
Bipartisan agreement against importing foreign beef protects regional cattle ranchers, demonstrating that local agricultural preservation can momentarily transcend national partisan loyalty when economic pressure is acute.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The debate commits a WHAT vs WHO plane switch. Leaders sell tariffs and strikes as macroeconomic defense (WHAT), but the physical costs fall entirely on working farmers and fuel consumers (WHO) while politicians hoard power.

Social Physics Analysis:
Boebert runs a selfish loop, cloaking power hoarding behind security pretexts to deflect from fuel inflation. Laubacher offers transparency on rural costs, yet both deploy post-hoc justifications to prioritize personal ambition over farm stability.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil. Prioritizing unvetted executive strikes and trade friction systematically contracts rural solvency.

The Unavoidable Truth: Working farmers and everyday consumers shoulder the brutal financial fallout of foreign trade conflicts and energy spikes.
The Unavoidable Lie: Tariffs are paid by foreign rivals rather than taxing domestic supply chains.

Alethekanon:
When congressional representatives surrender war powers and defend trade taxes, representation degenerates into partisan insulation. True accountability demands defending constituent economic survival over uncritical loyalty to the executive.

Awwthekanon:
My heart goes out to the farming families staring at diesel bills and wondering how to finish harvest. They work the soil to feed our country, and they deserve leaders who listen to their struggles rather than playing partisan musical chairs with their livelihoods.

Brothekanon:
Bro, watching two politicians who just moved into the district argue about diesel prices while farmers get crushed is peak politics. One defends taxes on our own stuff and the other just swapped jerseys to get elected. Regular folks keep footing the bill.

Spirithekanon:
"The people starve because those above them eat too much in taxes." Tao Te Ching 75 FAIL
When leaders inflict crushing tariffs and fuel inflation on working farmers to fund geopolitical conflict, they destroy the foundation of the state.

Lauren Boebert, Eileen Laubacher talk tariffs and inflation during televised debate

The two women vying to represent Colorado’s easternmost congressional district engaged in a feisty back-and-forth during a televised debate Monday night, touching on topics ranging from tariffs to the Iran war to diesel prices.

Actual Article Body:

Trending:

The two women vying to represent Colorado’s easternmost congressional district engaged in a feisty back-and-forth during a televised debate Monday night, touching on topics ranging from tariffs to the Iran war to diesel prices.

The candidates, incumbent Congresswoman Lauren Boebert and retired Navy rear admiral Eileen Laubacher, also waded into more arcane topics like Laubacher’s previous work history and Boebert’s vote against a bill to help veterans.

On the Iran war, which has driven up diesel prices to record levels in recent weeks, Boebert, a 39-year-old Republican, said she hadn’t wanted for the country to be at war but stands by President Donald Trump.

“I will stand by and say the president is commander in chief,” she said. “This was never about regime change — this was about making sure Iran never has a nuclear weapon.”

Laubacher, a 58-year-old Democrat who served in the Navy for 34 years, said the United States and Iran were in negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program when Trump bombed the country on Feb. 28.

“When negotiations are on the table, you do not start a war,” Laubacher said. “We should have given those serious efforts and instead of that, we go to war and we accidentally kill 150 girls (at an Iranian school).”

Boebert and Laubacher appeared together in the 9News studios for the hour-long debate — the only one scheduled in the district this fall. The election is Nov. 3 and thousands of ballots have already landed in Colorado voters’ mailboxes.

Democrats are taking their hardest run yet at the district that covers all or parts of 21 Colorado counties that stretch largely across the state’s Eastern Plains. Pieces of several populous Front Range counties, like Arapahoe, Douglas, Larimer and El Paso, are also in the 4th District.

The district has been reliably red for years, with no Democrat representing it since Betsy Markey left Congress in January 2011 after serving a single term.

But the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added the 4th to its list of “Districts in Play” in August. It’s part of an aggressive play the national party has made this election cycle for House districts once considered out of reach, taking advantage of the president’s plummeting poll ratings over the Iran war and stubbornly elevated prices.

The 4th Congressional District is dominated by farming and ranching, where Trump’s tariffs haven’t always been greeted with enthusiasm. Boebert on Monday insisted that Trump’s tariffs have been a “tool” in trying to secure the best trade deals for the United States.

But Laubacher said many of the Trump administration’s tariffs are not paid by foreign governments, but by Americans.

“It’s hurting our consumers,” she said. “Congress is supposed to be looking after consumers.”

Laubacher was challenged by the moderator as to why she only switched her party affiliation from Republican to Democrat in the last year or so. And whether her decision to do so was solely for the purposes of running for Congress.

Laubacher said her previous Republican affiliation was due to the fact that the party traditionally emphasized fiscal restraint, a strong military defense and support for individual liberties.

“I feel like we’ve gone from that party to a party that is barely recognizable,” she said of today’s GOP.

Boebert was asked about whether she has made a concerted effort to engage in less drama-filled and confrontational behavior, antics that landed her in hot water — and her name splashed across front pages everywhere — when she was tossed from a musical three years ago after fellow patrons objected to her conduct in public.

“I think it’s great to have an approach to disagree better,” Boebert said.

The women agreed on a couple of items: both said the loose border policy under President Biden was a disaster and both said it was a mistake for Trump to import Argentinian beef in an effort to bring down meat prices.

Laubacher holds a massive money advantage over Boebert. According to the most recent contributions and expenditures listed with the Federal Election Commission, which date back to the end of June, Laubacher had nearly 15 times as much money on hand as did her opponent.

The latest fundraising reports, covering the third quarter of 2026, are due on Thursday.

Neither candidate has lived for long in the 4th District.

Boebert moved there last year after leaving her previous congressional district (the 3rd) in a successful move to save her political career. Laubacher moved to Highlands Ranch in 2024, having lived in the neighboring 7th Congressional District, where she still owns a home.
